chapter.name: Natural Resources and Their Use
chapter.blurb: When an element of Nature becomes a resource, how resources are categorised, why their uneven distribution shapes settlement, trade and conflict, and what responsible stewardship of them looks like.

scope_in.item: Explain when an element of Nature becomes a resource, using the three conditions: technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable
State the chapter's definition of natural resources and the special sense in which it uses the word exploitation
Categorise natural resources by the uses we put them to: essential for life, for materials, and for energy
Distinguish restoration from regeneration and describe Nature's no-waste cycle, including ecosystem functions and ecosystem services
Separate renewable from non-renewable resources and state the condition under which a renewable one stays renewable
Explain how uneven distribution of resources shapes settlements, trade, international relations and conflict, including the Kaveri sharing example
Explain the paradox of plenty and how India has generally avoided the resource curse
Describe the groundwater and soil-degradation problems and the Punjab caselet of over-extraction
Describe the pollution caused by cement production and the alternative and traditional materials being used instead
Outline what Vrikshayurveda advises and what the Sikkim organic-farming caselet achieved
Explain judicious use of non-renewables, the International Solar Alliance, unfair access to basic resources, and stewardship as lokasangraha

concepts.name: When Nature becomes a resource
concepts.description: The difference between Nature and a resource, the three conditions an element of Nature must meet before it counts as one, and the chapter's definition of natural resources.
concepts.idea: Nature is everything in our environment that humans did not create; it becomes a resource only when humans can actually reach it, afford it and are willing to use it.
concepts.rule: An element of Nature becomes a resource when it is technologically accessible, economically feasible to extract and culturally acceptable to use. All three must hold. In this chapter the word 'exploitation' simply means the extraction, utilisation and consumption of natural resources, with no negative sense. Natural resources are materials and substances that occur in Nature and are valuable to humans.
concepts.example: Trees exist on their own, but when we cut them and turn the wood into furniture we are treating the tree as a resource.

questions.a: In the first village the coal is a resource: the railway and power plant make it accessible and cheap to move, so the technological and economic conditions are met and nothing cultural stands in the way. In the second village the cost of moving coal without a railway may make extraction economically unfeasible, and the sacred grove makes it culturally unacceptable. questions.q: Design a simple three-question checklist a district officer could use to decide whether a newly found deposit in her district should be treated as a resource. Write each question and say what a 'no' answer to it would mean.
questions.a: Question 1: Do we have the technology to reach and extract it? A no means it stays a part of Nature for now, until technology improves. Question 2: Will the value of what we extract be greater than the cost of extracting it? A no means extraction would waste money and it should be left. Question 3: Do the people who live here accept its use? A no means the deposit must be left alone however cheap or easy extraction would be. Only if all three answers are yes is the deposit a resource.
s: Technological accessibility question written with its no meaning
Economic feasibility question written with its no meaning
Cultural acceptability question written with its no meaning
Stated that all three must be yes for the deposit to count as a resource

concepts.name: Categorising natural resources by use
concepts.description: Why we categorise at all, and the chapter's first criterion: grouping natural resources by the uses we put them to.
concepts.idea: A category is a shortcut for talking about a whole set of things at once, and resources can be grouped by what we use them for.
concepts.rule: We categorise by choosing shared characteristics, called criteria, and naming the groups so a whole set can be referred to in one word. One criterion for natural resources is the use we put them to, which gives three groups: resources essential for life such as air, water and the food grown in soil; resources for materials such as wood, marble, coal and gold; and resources for energy such as coal, water, petroleum, natural gas, sunlight and wind.
concepts.example: A piece of wood can be made into a chair for utility or carved into a statuette for beauty, so wood is a resource for materials.

questions.a: Both have a point. Still air is what we breathe, which makes it essential for life; moving air is wind, which the chapter lists as a source of energy. questions.q: The chapter says shared names and meanings help us communicate more effectively. Judge how useful the three use-based categories would be to a town planner deciding what to protect first, and give reasons.
questions.a: They are useful as a first sort, because the category of resources essential for life immediately marks out air, water and soil as the things a town cannot do without and must protect first. They are less useful beyond that, because they say nothing about whether a resource will run out, which is what the renewable and non-renewable criterion adds. So the planner should use them to set priorities, then apply a second criterion.

concepts.name: Restoration, regeneration and Nature's cycles
concepts.description: How Nature heals and renews itself, why its cycles produce no waste, what breaks those cycles, and the difference between ecosystem functions and ecosystem services.
concepts.idea: Nature repairs itself and creates new life, and in a healthy cycle nothing is left over as waste.
concepts.rule: Restoration is returning something to its original healthy state after it has been degraded or damaged; regeneration goes further and is Nature's ability to create new life and the conditions for thriving. In Nature's cycles there is no waste, because what one process discards another consumes. An ecosystem function is what Nature does anyway, such as a forest filtering water or preventing soil erosion; it is called an ecosystem service when humans benefit from it. A mature tree produces about 275 litres of oxygen a day while a person needs about 350 litres.
concepts.example: A fallen tree is fed on by bacteria, fungi and insects, becomes part of the soil and enriches it, and new plants grow from seeds in that soil.

questions.q: A colony of 40 people wants to grow enough mature trees to match the oxygen its residents use. Using the figures in this chapter, work out roughly how many trees that would take, show your working, and say why the real answer is not this simple.
questions.a: Each person needs about 350 litres of oxygen a day, so 40 people need about 40 times 350, that is about 14000 litres a day. Each mature tree gives about 275 litres a day, so the number of trees is about 14000 divided by 275, which is roughly 51 trees. The real answer is not this simple because the chapter says both figures vary: oxygen output depends on the type of tree, and a person's need changes with activity, height and weight.

questions.q: Two rivers run past two towns. Below one town the river still supports fish; below the other it does not. Using Nature's cycle of restoration and regeneration, analyse what is most likely different about the waste each town produces, and what this means for the people downstream.
questions.a: The waste of the first town is probably the kind that can decay and become food for some lifeform, so Nature's cycle absorbs it and the river restores itself. The waste of the second town is probably industrial waste that cannot decay, so the cycle is broken and the river becomes poisonous and cannot support life. Downstream of the first town people still get water and fish, which are ecosystem services; downstream of the second they lose both, and the damage will not repair itself while the discharge continues.
s: First town's waste identified as decaying into food for some lifeform

questions.q: 'Nature will always repair whatever we damage, so we need not worry.' Judge this claim using what the chapter says about restoration, regeneration and industrial waste.
questions.a: The claim is only half true. Nature does restore and regenerate, as a healing cut and a forest recovering after a wildfire show. But the chapter also says that irresponsible human actions have disturbed many of Nature's cycles, and that industrial waste which cannot decay leaves a river poisonous and unable to support life. Nature repairs only while its rhythm is left intact, so the claim cannot be relied on.
s: The true part acknowledged with an example of restoration
The limit named, that cycles can be disturbed by human action
Verdict given that the claim cannot be relied on, with the waste example

questions.q: Design a poster for your school that teaches the difference between an ecosystem function and an ecosystem service. Describe what you would draw, what you would label as functions, what you would label as services, and the one sentence you would print at the bottom.
questions.a: I would draw a forest on a hillside with a village below it. On the village side I would label the services: clean water in the taps, farmland that has not washed away and crops pollinated by insects from the forest. An arrow would run from each function to the service it produces. At the bottom I would print: Nature does this anyway; it becomes a service the moment it reaches us.
s: A clear drawing described that separates the forest from the people

concepts.name: Renewable and non-renewable resources
concepts.description: The chapter's second criterion for categorising resources, the condition a renewable resource must meet to stay renewable, and why non-renewables must be used judiciously.
concepts.idea: A resource is renewable only for as long as we take it no faster than Nature can replace it.
concepts.rule: Renewable resources such as solar energy, wind energy, energy from flowing water and timber from forests keep returning, but only while the natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration is not disturbed. Non-renewable resources are created over long periods and cannot be replenished at the rate we use them; these include the fossil fuels coal and petroleum and minerals and metals such as iron, copper and gold. India's coal reserves have been estimated to last another 50 years.
concepts.example: If we harvest timber faster than the forest can grow trees, we will eventually deplete the forest, and the renewable resource stops renewing.

questions.q: Tuna keep the ocean ecosystem in balance by eating smaller fish and shrimps, yet their numbers are falling. Explain how commercial over-fishing turned a renewable resource into a shrinking one, what was tried in response, and why the decline has still not stopped.
questions.a: Tuna are renewable while the natural rhythm of breeding is respected, which is why communities traditionally refrained from fishing during the spawning season. Commercialisation removed that restraint and led to over-fishing, so the catch outran the rate at which the population could regenerate. In response some agreements were reached to control fishing. The decline nevertheless continues, which shows that agreements alone do not restore a population once the rhythm of regeneration has been broken, and the loss matters because tuna keep the ocean ecosystem in balance.
s: Traditional restraint during the spawning season described
Commercialisation and over-fishing identified as outrunning regeneration
Agreements on control of fishing named as the response

questions.q: Two districts depend on the same river. One protects the forest at the river's head; the other clears it for farmland. Analyse what is likely to happen to the river in each district over thirty years, and explain why the same resource behaves differently.
questions.a: In the protected district the forest keeps renewing itself and holds and releases water, so the river continues to flow and stays a renewable resource. In the cleared district the forest can no longer renew itself, the soil is not held, and clearing forests is one of the factors the chapter links to rising temperatures and faster glacier melt, so the river becomes less reliable. The river water is renewable in both places only in principle; what differs is whether the natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration has been left intact, and it is human action, not the resource, that decides this.
s: Outcome in the protected district described with the forest renewing itself
Outcome in the cleared district described with the loss of renewal

questions.q: 'Renewable resources can never be exhausted.' Judge this statement using the chapter's examples of timber and tuna.
questions.a: The statement is wrong. Timber is renewable, but if we harvest it faster than the forest can grow trees we will eventually deplete the forest. Tuna are renewable, but commercial over-fishing has driven their numbers into decline despite agreements to control fishing. A renewable resource can be exhausted whenever the rate of use overtakes the rate of regeneration.
s: Verdict given that the statement is wrong

Tuna example used to show depletion by over-fishing

questions.q: Write a short set of rules a fishing village could adopt so that its catch stays renewable. Give three rules and explain, for each one, the natural rhythm it protects.
questions.a: Rule one: no fishing during the spawning season, which protects the rhythm by which the fish population replaces itself. Rule two: a fixed limit on the catch each month, set below the rate at which the stock recovers, so that use never overtakes regeneration. Rule three: leave the smallest fish and return them to the water, so that young fish live long enough to breed. Together these keep the take below the rate of renewal, which is the condition the chapter gives for a resource to stay renewable.
s: A spawning-season rule written with the rhythm it protects
A catch-limit rule written with the rhythm it protects
A third workable rule written with the rhythm it protects
Rules tied back to keeping use below the rate of regeneration

concepts.name: Distribution of resources, its implications and the paradox of plenty
concepts.description: Why natural resources are spread unevenly, how that shapes settlement, trade, relations and conflict, and why abundance alone does not make a country prosperous.
concepts.idea: Where a resource happens to lie shapes who settles, who trades and who quarrels, but having plenty of it guarantees nothing.
concepts.rule: Natural resources are not evenly distributed across the planet or even within a country, and this shapes human settlements, trade patterns, international relations and conflicts. Industries near a resource bring employment, townships and better facilities, but also displacement and threats to sacred places. Nature ignores political boundaries, so rivers must be shared by negotiation, as with the Kaveri. Abundance does not guarantee prosperity: economists call this the natural resource curse or the paradox of plenty, and it happens when a country cannot build industries that convert its resources into products of higher value.
concepts.example: The Kaveri river water is shared among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry, and it took negotiations and deft management to keep the peace.

questions.q: The chapter says that human knowledge, good governance and strategic planning decide whether resources become lasting benefits or temporary windfalls. Analyse what a temporary windfall would look like in a mining district after thirty years, and what a lasting benefit would look like instead.
questions.a: A temporary windfall would mean the ore has been dug out and sold raw, the mine has closed, the jobs have gone, the township has emptied and the district is left with damaged land, displaced families and nothing of higher value built from the resource. A lasting benefit would mean industries were built that turned the ore into products worth more, so skills, factories and incomes remain after the deposit is worked out, and extraction was balanced against sustainability along the way. The difference is not the size of the deposit but whether knowledge, governance and planning were applied to it.

s: Verdict given that the claim is not sound

concepts.name: Stewardship of renewables: groundwater, soil and the Punjab caselet
concepts.description: What stewardship means, how groundwater and soil are being pushed past their capacity to regenerate, and the Punjab caselet of over-extraction.
concepts.idea: Groundwater and soil are renewable, but only at Nature's pace, and India is drawing on both far faster than that.
concepts.rule: Stewardship means using resources so that renewables can restore and regenerate and non-renewables are used judiciously. In most states groundwater is extracted faster than the water table is replenished, so the deficit builds up, extraction costs rise and the water eventually becomes unavailable. Improper use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides degrades soil. In Punjab, high-yielding wheat and paddy from the 1960s, free power and heavy chemical use together left groundwater inaccessible to depths of about 30 metres, with chemicals dissolved in it, and almost 80 per cent of the state classified as over-exploited.
concepts.example: Water harvesting, rejuvenating ponds and tanks, cutting wasteful use and reusing processed water are the strategies being tried to raise groundwater levels again.

questions.a: Free power meant that pumping water cost the farmer nothing, so there was no reason to limit it. This led to over-pumping of groundwater, a situation the chapter says is still prevalent in much of India. Because the pumping ran far ahead of the rate at which the water table is replenished, the water level fell until it became inaccessible to depths of about 30 metres in a large part of the state.

Link made to the falling water table and its depth

questions.q: Punjab's Green Revolution fed a large part of the country, yet the state now faces a groundwater crisis. Explain how one set of changes produced both results.
questions.a: From the 1960s farmers shifted to high-yielding varieties of wheat and paddy, which raised output so far that India became self-sufficient in food. The same varieties needed much more water than traditional seeds, free power made pumping it costless, and modern techniques brought chemical fertilisers and pesticides. The gain in food and the loss of groundwater came from exactly the same changes, which is why food security was ensured for the short term while the long-term consequences will take time and effort to heal.
s: The shift to high-yielding varieties and the rise in food output described
The extra water demand, free power and chemicals identified
Conclusion that the same changes produced both the gain and the crisis

questions.q: A district in another state is starting down the same path as Punjab: free power for pumps, high-yielding paddy and heavy fertiliser use. Write four steps the district could take now, and explain for each one the part of the Punjab story it would avoid.
questions.a: One, charge at least something for the power used to pump, so that pumping is not costless and the over-pumping that emptied Punjab's aquifer does not begin. Two, choose crops matched to the district's rainfall instead of water-hungry paddy, avoiding the extra demand the high-yielding varieties created. Three, harvest rainwater and rejuvenate the ponds and tanks, so that recharge keeps pace with extraction and no deficit builds up. Four, replace part of the chemical input with cow dung, mulching and multi-cropping, so that the soil is not degraded and chemicals do not dissolve into the groundwater and cause health hazards.
s: A step on the cost of power with the over-pumping it avoids
A step on crop choice with the water demand it avoids
A step on recharge with the deficit it avoids
A step on soil and chemicals with the degradation or health hazard it avoids

questions.q: The chapter says food security was ensured for the short term but the long-term consequences will take time and effort to heal. Analyse what was gained and what was lost in Punjab, and explain why the two cannot simply be added up.
questions.a: What was gained was food: the Green Revolution fed a large proportion of the population and helped India become self-sufficient, and that gain was immediate and measurable. What was lost was the groundwater of a whole state, now inaccessible to about 30 metres across a large area with almost 80 per cent of the state over-exploited, along with soil health and clean water for drinking. The two cannot simply be added up because they are of different kinds and different times: the food was consumed within a season, while the aquifer took far longer to fill and may not refill in a lifetime, and the health hazards fall on people who never chose the policy.

A policy that helps in the short term can damage the resource it depends on, so support for farmers needs to be designed so that it does not reward waste.
s: The benefit of the policy acknowledged

questions.q: Design a water plan for your own school that would help the local water table. Include one harvesting measure, one reuse measure and one measure to cut waste, and say how you would show that the plan is working.
questions.a: Harvesting: channel the rain from the roofs into a recharge pit beside the playground so that it soaks into the ground instead of running off. Reuse: collect the water from the hand-wash basins, let it settle, and use it on the school garden instead of fresh water. Cutting waste: fit push taps that close by themselves and repair every leak within a week, since wasteful consumption is one of the things the chapter asks us to cut. To show it is working I would record the depth of the water in the school borewell on the same date each month and the monthly water bill, and compare the readings year to year.
s: A harvesting measure described
A reuse measure described
A measure to cut wasteful consumption described
A way of checking the plan is working described

concepts.name: Sustainable materials, traditional knowledge and judicious use of non-renewables
concepts.description: Cement pollution and the alternatives to it, Vrikshayurveda and the Sikkim organic caselet, and the switch to renewable energy alongside fair access and stewardship.
concepts.idea: Old knowledge combined with new technology gives materials and farming that pollute less, while non-renewables must be stretched until better alternatives arrive.
concepts.rule: Cement production is one of the most polluting industries: its fine dust harms lungs, settles on leaves and reduces yields, and pollutes soil and water, which is why the Central Pollution Control Board has issued guidelines and why stone, mud, plant-based and recycled materials are being revived. Vrikshayurveda is an ancient Indian botanical science of plants and trees, formalised in texts such as Surapala's Vrikshayurveda around the 10th century CE. Sikkim became a 100 per cent organic state in 2016. Non-renewables must be used so they last until sustainable alternatives are found, and access to basic resources such as water and clean air is often unfair to some sections of society.
concepts.example: India and France launched the International Alliance for Solar Energy in 2015, a coalition of sunshine-rich countries, and the Bhadla Solar Park became a symbol of India's solar ambitions.

questions.q: The chapter says access to resources as basic as water and clean air is often unfair to some sections of society. Analyse who is worst affected in a city, why they are worst affected, and how this connects to the idea of lokasangraha.
questions.a: Those worst affected are the people in city areas that do not receive an adequate and regular supply of drinking water, and those who cannot protect themselves from air pollution caused by industries and the excessive use of fossil fuels. They are worst affected because they have the least means to buy their way out, by tankers, filters or moving away, so the same polluted air and short supply hurt them far more than others. Lokasangraha, which the chapter takes from the Bhagavad Gita, is the idea that everyone must transcend personal desires and act for the wellbeing of all, and it answers this directly: stewardship is not only about the quantity of a resource but about who gets it, and a society acting for the wellbeing of all would fix the unequal access first.
s: Those with inadequate water supply or no protection from air pollution identified
Reason given that they have least means to protect themselves
Lokasangraha explained as acting for the wellbeing of all
Connection drawn between fair access and stewardship

questions.q: One solar park in Rajasthan can meet about 15 per cent of that state's current electricity needs. Judge how far solar parks alone can solve India's energy problem, and give reasons.
questions.a: They can take us a long way but not the whole way. One park meeting about 15 per cent of a single state's current needs shows the scale is real, and India has abundant sunshine and is leading the International Alliance for Solar Energy. But the figure is of current needs, and the chapter says demand keeps rising as the population expands and development accelerates, so a share of today's need is a smaller share of tomorrow's. Solar must therefore be combined with wind, flowing water and the judicious use of what coal remains.
s: A clear judgement given rather than a flat yes or no
The strength of the figure and India's solar advantage used
The limitation named, such as rising demand or the need for other sources

questions.q: Your school is to be rebuilt. Write a brief for the architect that follows this chapter: name the materials you want used, the energy source for the building, one traditional idea you want respected, and the one sentence of purpose you want written on the foundation stone.
questions.a: Materials: mud and local stone wherever the structure allows, with plant-based and recycled materials from waste plastic for fittings, so that we use as little cement as possible. Energy: solar panels on every roof, since our region has abundant sunshine and the chapter asks us to switch to renewable sources for as many purposes as we can. Traditional idea: the Vrikshayurveda approach to the garden, with plants matched to our soil, mixed cropping and ploughing that keeps the soil moist and alive. Foundation stone: 'Built for the wellbeing of all, from what this place already gives.'
s: Low-cement or traditional and recycled materials specified
A renewable energy source specified with a reason
A traditional idea from the chapter named and applied
A sentence of purpose written that reflects stewardship
